title: What Spanking Does
text:
For generations, many parents have believed that an occasional spanking teaches children to behave. Researchers had studied the question for decades, but critics argued that earlier reviews mixed spanking with harsher forms of physical abuse.

In 2016, Elizabeth Gershoff of the University of Texas at Austin and Andrew Grogan-Kaylor of the University of Michigan published new meta-analyses that focused narrowly on spanking, defined as hitting a child on the bottom or the limbs with an open hand. They combined the results of 75 studies covering more than 160,000 children.

The pattern was consistent. Spanking was linked to worse outcomes on most of the measures they examined, including more aggression, more antisocial behavior, more mental health problems, lower self-esteem, lower cognitive ability and poorer relationships between parent and child. Spanking was not linked to better behavior or greater compliance over time. The associations held in studies that followed children over time, and they looked similar to the associations found for physical abuse, only weaker.

The researchers also found that adults who had been spanked as children were more likely to support spanking their own children, suggesting how the practice passes from one generation to the next.
lesson: Spanking is linked to worse behavior, not better, across many studies. Clear limits, calm consequences and explanation are safer tools.
location: University of Texas at Austin and University of Michigan, USA
source: Gershoff, E. T., and Grogan-Kaylor, A. (2016). Spanking and child outcomes: Old controversies and new meta-analyses. Journal of Family Psychology, 30(4), 453-469.
caveat: The studies were correlational, and some researchers argue that difficult behavior in children may partly cause spanking rather than only result from it.
